newsitem.title: UK: UK's lax tax makes it top for oil explorers - poll.
newsitem.headline: UK's lax tax makes it top for oil explorers - poll.

text.p: Britain's benign oil tax regime still makes it the world's most attractive country for oil explorers despite the remote chance of a big crude find, according to an oil company survey released on Friday.

A poll of oil company interest in new ventures in 146 oil producing nations saw Britain top the list ahead of Venezuela, which led the poll last year, the survey by upstream advisors Robertson Research International found.

"The attractive fiscal environment for petroleum producers in the UK together with the progressive licensing regulations continue to interest both established producers/explorers and new international players, in investing in further exploration ventures," the survey said.

Britain's favourable taxation and licensing regime outweighed the potential for much bigger oilfield finds in other countries. Britain's large oil fields are now reaching maturity and most exploration centres on relatively small prospects.
The survey elicited responses from 111 oil companies, covering some 75 percent of total oil company international upstream spending for the year.
Indonesia, having made its fiscal regime more attractive, came third on the survey. Also in the top 10 were Algeria, Australia, Colombia, Argentina, Peru, Angola and Iraq.
Robertson said Russia and its former Soviet neighbours fell down the rankings making the region the world's least popular for oil explorers.
Uncertain regulatory regimes and high taxation more than outweigh the prospects for massive finds in Russia.
The poll reported that 80 percent of companies indicated that their worldwide exploration and production budgets would increase on 1996.
Budgets were based on an oil price projection more than $2 higher than last year. The companies polled on average budgeted for an $18.64 oil price compared to $16.48 for 1996.
North Sea Brent crude last year averaged $20.32 from $16.95 in 1995.
